newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Irish tax cuts seen as govt reaps revenue harvest.
newsitem.headline: Irish tax cuts seen as govt reaps revenue harvest.

text.p: The Irish government looks well placed to cut taxes in its election budget in early 1997 after the exchequer reported a sizeable surplus in end-September returns on Wednesday, analysts said.

Finance minister Ruairi Quinn said a surplus at this stage of the year was unprecedented in a generation and stated that the Exchequer Borrowing Requirement (EBR) for 1996 was set to emerge well below the budget target of 729 million punts.
A spokesman for the Department of Finance told reporters at a briefing that he expected the government to undershoot the annual EBR target by around 300 million punts.

The Department reported a cumulative running surplus of 185 million punts to end-September in its third quarter exchequer returns data. Economists' forecasts ranged from zero to a 175 million punt surplus.
Irish bonds surged after the release of the returns and bond dealers said the market had taken the figures well and expected further gains on Thursday morning.
"I think the figures were very good for the economy. They show that funding is positively very strong at the moment ... more gains can be expected tomorrow," one dealer said.
The coalition government of Prime Minister John Bruton will unveil its last budget in January next year before elections which must be held by November 1977.
Some analysts believe a snap election could be called after a give-away budget early next year.
Goodbody economist Han de Jong said the figures were much in line with expectations. De Jong had forecast a surplus of 175 million punts.

Davy economist Oliver Mangan said the government had achieved such a big undershoot in the EBR because of much stronger than expected tax revenue, which basically reflected the strength of economic activity.
"Given the state of the public finances now, scope for significant tax cuts ahead of an election budget will probably be too difficult for the Minister of Finance to resist," Mangan said.
Tax revenue was up 10.7 percent year-on-year in the first nine months of the year. This compares with a forecast increase for the whole year of 6.5 percent.

"Today's figures are very encouraging," Bloxham stockbrokers economist Alan McQuaid said. "While the debt reduction in the first three quarters may be in part due to timing factors it still nevertheless emphasises the government's strong budgetary position."
McQuaid agreed tax cuts were on the horizon and anticipated the standard tax rate be cut to 25 percent and the top rate to 47 percent.

Economists said the only constraint on the government will be the fear that generous tax cuts may lead to unwanted inflationary pressures in the year when the European Union takes stock of who qualifies for European Monetary Union.
Maastricht's requirements state qualifying countries should have an inflation rate not more that 1.5 per cent higher than the three best performing states.
McQuaid is forecasting an inflation rate of 2.5 percent for Ireland in 1997. He estimates the current EU average at around 1.3 to 1.5 percent.
